summary: "Changing the Python hash seed shifts up to 17% of an agent's attack verdicts and moves attack success rate by 19 points — TARE shows most agent-security benchmark numbers are not attributable to the agent, the attack or the defense."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-11-24-tare-content-free-state-attribution.svg"
---

Security benchmarks for LLM agents record whether each attack succeeded, and compare agents, attacks and defenses by **attack success rate (ASR)**. Such a comparison is only meaningful if the agent, the attack and the defense actually *cause* each verdict. Abdelmonaim Bounite and Zangir Iklassov (MBZUAI, Abu Dhabi) show that verdicts also depend on **content-free state** — details of a run that carry no information about the system under test: the Python hash seed, the order of tools or evidence, the scoring of failed runs.

Because LLM-based gates and benchmark harnesses let whoever configures them choose this state, the authors treat it as **untrusted input** and require *decision noninterference*: it must influence no verdict. Their framework, **TARE** (Testing Attribution of Reported Effects), credits a reported effect to the agent, the attack or the defense only if it exceeds the measured influence of content-free state.

On **Agent Security Bench (ASB)** the effect is stark. With a fixed hash seed, runs are identical for seven agents from four model families. Change the seed and **up to 17% of an agent's verdicts flip**, while ASR moves by at most 5 points. The seed acts through tool order: sorting the tool list instead of reverse-sorting it **raises ASR by up to 19 points**, because ASB's naming convention puts attacker tools first — an ordering artifact, not a property of the attack. When the same evidence is merely reordered, **six of seven LLM judges change their decision on 17–91% of 98 proposed actions**.

The consequence for headline numbers is direct. Across eighteen agent-defense combinations, TARE's worst-case test attributes effects to only **two of three defenses** — and one of them in opposite directions on two agents. A test fixed in advance confirms a 4.8-point decrease from the third. In those attributed decreases, **35–69% of the stopped attacks end without any tool call**, which ASB nonetheless counts as a failed attack.

Caveat: TARE measures attribution, not verdict correctness, and it does not fix ASB. But it makes the uncomfortable point that a reproducible benchmark score is not automatically an attributable one — a distinction every agent-security leaderboard currently elides.

Source: [arXiv:2611.30259 — Attributing Security Outcomes in LLM-Agent Evaluations: The Role of Content-Free State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.30259)
